name: DeepWaterMap and WatNet pretrained surface-water CNNs

identity.method_name: DeepWaterMap v2 (Isikdogan et al.) and WatNet (Luo, Tong & Hu) -- two purpose-built, pretrained surface-water segmentation CNNs
identity.core_idea: Both are fully convolutional networks trained end-to-end elsewhere and released with fixed weights for direct inference: DeepWaterMap is a compact fully convolutional encoder-decoder trained on a global Landsat-derived surface-water dataset to output a binary/probabilistic water mask robust to cloud and shadow; WatNet uses a DeepLabv3+ decoder over a MobileNetV2 backbone trained on the Earth Surface Water Dataset (global rivers and lakes from Sentinel-2) to output a Sentinel-2-native water mask. Neither requires any local training -- both are run as a single forward pass per scene, which is their entire appeal against the project's zero-ground-truth constraint.
identity.official_dataset_ids: Neither model corresponds to a Google Earth Engine or other formal catalog dataset ID. DeepWaterMap's training data is a custom global Landsat surface-water compilation distributed by the author (no catalog ID; see github.com/isikdogan/deepwatermap). WatNet's training data is the 'Earth Surface Water Dataset,' Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.5205674 -- a citable dataset DOI but not a GEE/official product ID.

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Transfer from another labelled dataset, used zero-shot. Both networks were fit on external, independently-labelled surface-water data (global Landsat scenes for DeepWaterMap, the global Earth Surface Water Dataset for WatNet) and are applied directly to the project's Bengaluru scenes with no local fine-tuning and no local labels at all. Cost is near zero in labelling effort; the cost instead is unverified domain transfer, since neither training set is known to include hyacinth-choked, seasonally-desilted, tropical urban lakes.
fit_to_project.input_required: DeepWaterMap expects 6 bands approximately matching Landsat B2-B7 (Blue, Green, Red, NIR, SWIR1, SWIR2). WatNet explicitly requires Sentinel-2 bands B2, B3, B4, B8, B11, and B12 in that order (four 10 m visible/NIR bands plus two 20 m SWIR bands). CRITICAL FINDING: the project's cached six bands are B02, B03, B04, B08, B11, and SCL -- B12 (SWIR2) is absent from the cache for BOTH models. Neither model can be run as specified from the currently cached bands; B12 would need to be re-pulled from the Earth Search STAC archive. This is not a fundamental blocker (B12 is a standard Sentinel-2 L2A band and is trivially fetchable from the same source as the other five), but it means the 'six bands already cached' are not sufficient as they stand, contrary to what a quick read of the note might suggest.
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: yes, in the narrow model-fitting sense -- no local training occurs at all, so the 42-lake-year sample-size question does not constrain model fitting; inference is one forward pass per scene, i.e. 42 independent inference runs. The same downstream constraint as the current baseline still applies once the resulting per-year water-area numbers are folded back into the 42-row table for trend analysis.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes -- this is the defining appeal of the item, matching the project note exactly: both models ship pretrained and require zero local labels of any kind.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: Mismatched in two different ways. DeepWaterMap was trained on 30 m Landsat imagery; applying it to the project's 20 m Sentinel-2 grid is a resolution mismatch in the finer direction. The README states the model 'does not require... Landsat-7, Landsat-8, or Sentinel-2 images specifically' and claims robustness to sensor spectral shifts, but this claim is not empirically demonstrated for 20 m Sentinel-2 SWIR-resampled bands over small tropical lakes and should be treated as an unverified transfer claim, not a guarantee. WatNet was trained natively on Sentinel-2, working at its 10 m visible/NIR resolution with the 20 m SWIR bands upsampled to 10 m for input; the project's grid has already been resampled down to a uniform 20 m, i.e. coarser than WatNet's native working resolution, discarding exactly the resolution WatNet's own pipeline expects for B2/B3/B4/B8. Net effect: WatNet is the closer match of the two since it is Sentinel-2-native, but neither model exactly matches the project's fixed 20 m EPSG:32643 grid as currently built.
fit_to_project.label_source_needed: none -- both are pretrained and used purely for inference.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: None of the four directly. Does not add rows to the 42-row table, does not touch the static OpenStreetMap-buildings problem, does not create independent ground truth (a model prediction is not verified truth, it is simply another unverified estimate alongside the project's own MNDWI baseline), and does not add extra scenes per year beyond the single dry-season scene the project already has.
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No. Like the current MNDWI baseline, both models produce a single-date water/no-water mask with no temporal or contextual awareness; a drained lake bed reads as 'not water' in exactly the same way an encroached, permanently filled lake bed would. Neither model has any built-in mechanism to distinguish the two.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: No, and this is the item's central weakness for this project. Both are surface-*water* extraction networks, not water-vs-vegetation-vs-built-up classifiers; a hyacinth mat is green and vegetated, which is exactly the signal both models are trained to classify as 'not water,' directly reproducing the project's current MNDWI/NDVI confound (Bellandur 2019: 16 ha water vs 260 ha vegetation inside a 315 ha footprint) rather than resolving it. Neither model has a 'vegetated water' or macrophyte class of any kind.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None -- the output is a raw water mask with the same OpenStreetMap-proxy-only status as the current method; neither model's output changes what boundary or buffer distance the project ultimately overlays it against.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: The models' weights are fixed and never retrained, but the water mask each model produces is recomputed fresh per scene, so the derived water/no-water label does genuinely vary year to year in the sense the current baseline already does -- this is not a new capability relative to the existing method, just the same property delivered by a different (external, pretrained) classifier.

implementation.libraries: DeepWaterMap: TensorFlow/Keras (original repo is TF1-style with a documented TF2-compatible inference path); WatNet: TensorFlow/Keras (DeepLabv3+/MobileNetV2 implemented in TF). Both need rasterio/numpy for band stacking and normalisation in the exact band order each model expects.
implementation.pretrained_weights: Both ship ready-to-use checkpoints hosted directly in their official GitHub repositories. DeepWaterMap: checkpoint cp.135.ckpt, the result of training on the full global Landsat-derived dataset for 135 epochs, including additional harder cloud-cover samples beyond the original published paper's set (github.com/isikdogan/deepwatermap). WatNet: pretrained model weights trained on the Earth Surface Water Dataset (Sentinel-2, global rivers and lakes, Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.5205674), hosted in github.com/xinluo2018/WatNet.
implementation.licence: [uncertain] [verify] Neither github.com/isikdogan/deepwatermap nor github.com/xinluo2018/WatNet displays an explicit LICENSE file at the repository root at the time of checking in this session (direct fetch of a LICENSE path on both repos returned 404). Absence of an explicit open-source licence is a real academic-use risk: by default, all rights are reserved to the author unless stated otherwise, even though the code and weights are publicly downloadable. This should be flagged to the guide and, if used, either the authors should be contacted for explicit permission, or a community-maintained fork with a stated licence should be used instead (e.g. github.com/giswqs/deep-water-map, a mirror of DeepWaterMap maintained by the segment-geospatial/leafmap author, which may carry different licensing terms and should be checked independently before use).
implementation.compute_requirement: CPU-only inference is genuinely feasible for both -- these are lightweight pretrained CNNs designed for scene-level batch inference rather than training. Running inference over all 42 scenes takes minutes on a laptop CPU; no GPU, Colab, or Kaggle session is required at all for this item, which is a real practical advantage over both A1 (needs a training loop) and A3 (benefits strongly from a GPU).
implementation.student_days: Roughly 2-4 student-days total: environment setup for two separate TensorFlow codebases, resolving the missing-B12-band gap by re-fetching that band from the STAC archive, adapting each model's expected input band order and reflectance normalisation, running inference over 42 scenes, and sanity-checking the outputs visually against the existing MNDWI baseline. This is the cheapest of the three A-group items by a wide margin.

evaluation.metrics: IoU/F1 against a small manually spot-checked reference set (since no ground truth exists, this is a visual-audit accuracy, not a true validation accuracy); the primary deliverable metric is the agreement/disagreement rate against the current MNDWI baseline per lake-year, and specifically whether either model changes the water-area number in a materially different direction on the two hyacinth-affected lakes (Bellandur, Varthur) and the desilted-year lakes (Bellandur 2021).
evaluation.validation_protocol: Not a train/test split in the traditional sense, because no local training occurs. The correct protocol is a stratified manual visual audit: select a deliberately stratified subset of lake-years (including at least one known desilting year -- Bellandur 2021 -- and the known hyacinth years -- Bellandur/Varthur 2019) and have a human check each model's output mask against a true-colour Sentinel-2 composite, reporting a qualitative agreement rate rather than a formal train/test accuracy.
evaluation.leakage_risk: Low from the 'no local training' angle, but a real, subtler leakage risk exists if the same MNDWI-derived pixels the project's own baseline treats as 'water' are then used as the reference for judging whether DeepWaterMap/WatNet are 'more accurate' -- that comparison is circular, since it would just measure agreement with the baseline being tested against, not agreement with ground truth. An independent cross-check, such as the JRC Global Surface Water monthly history (item D3 in the wider study) or manual visual labelling, is needed to break this circularity.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: No calibrated uncertainty from either model out of the box. Both output a per-pixel probability/logit that could be thresholded into a soft 'confidence' layer, but neither publication reports calibration against held-out ground truth, so this should not be presented as a statistically meaningful interval without post-hoc calibration (e.g. temperature scaling) or an ensemble of the two models' outputs treated as a 2-member disagreement band.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not applicable -- no local data augmentation or synthetic label expansion occurs in this item, since no local training happens; both models are used purely for inference on real, unmodified project imagery.

evidence.published_performance: DeepWaterMap: Isikdogan, Bovik & Passalacqua, 'Seeing Through the Clouds With DeepWaterMap,' IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters, 2020 (published online 2019), reports the v2 model achieves higher precision and recall than the original 2017 DeepWaterMap model on the same global Landsat benchmark, and can process a full Landsat scene in one shot [verify -- exact precision/recall/IoU figures were not independently retrievable from the accessible text in this session; the original 2017 paper 'Surface Water Mapping by Deep Learning,' IEEE JSTARS, reports its own separate numbers, also not independently confirmed here]. WatNet: Luo, Tong & Hu, 'An applicable and automatic method for earth surface water mapping based on multispectral images,' International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation, 103:102472, 2021, doi 10.1016/j.jag.2021.102472, is reported (via secondary summary) to achieve overall accuracies above 95% across selected test regions relative to AWEI, MNDWI, and OBIA baselines [verify -- exact per-region OA/F1/IoU table not independently confirmed from primary full text in this session].
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: DeepWaterMap: a global compilation of Landsat scenes, temperate/boreal-heavy by typical Landsat archive composition; no confirmed representation of Indian or tropical hyacinth-choked lakes [verify]. WatNet: the Earth Surface Water Dataset's global rivers and lakes, again with no confirmed representation of Indian urban lakes or macrophyte-dominated water bodies [verify]. Neither is a lake-scale study comparable to 6 individual Bengaluru lakes; both are large multi-site global benchmarks.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No evidence was found that either model has been validated on Indian lakes generally or Bengaluru lakes specifically, and no evidence was found that either has been tested against hyacinth-choked or seasonally-desilted urban water bodies. This is an unaddressed domain gap for both models as applied to this project.
evidence.evidence_recency: DeepWaterMap v2: 2019/2020 (the original 2017 version is pre-2020 and should not be cited as the current evidence). WatNet: 2021. Both fall before the 2023+ foundation-model era but are within the project's stated 2020-onward priority window; neither has more recent (2023-2025) validation located against a comparable domain.
evidence.primary_sources: DeepWaterMap repository: https://github.com/isikdogan/deepwatermap. DeepWaterMap v2 paper (Isikdogan, Bovik, Passalacqua, IEEE GRSL): https://www.isikdogan.com/files/isikdogan2019_deepwatermap_v2.pdf ; ADS abstract record: https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2020IGRSL..17.1662I/abstract. WatNet repository: https://github.com/xinluo2018/WatNet. WatNet paper (Luo, Tong & Hu, IJAEOG 2021): https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jag.2021.102472 ; ScienceDirect record: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0303243421001793. Earth Surface Water Dataset (Zenodo): https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5205674. WatNetv2 (extends to Landsat-5/7/8): https://github.com/xinluo2018/WatNetv2.

risk.failure_modes: The missing-B12 gap in the current cache silently breaks or forces a rework of both pipelines until B12 is re-fetched; domain shift to hyacinth mats, algal scum, and seasonally-exposed silty lake bed (none of which are known to be represented in either training set) is likely to produce systematic false negatives on precisely the two confounds this project cares about most (hyacinth and desilting); with no mechanism to flag 'vegetated water' versus 'bare dry land,' both models' output is likely to look qualitatively similar to, rather than a clear improvement over, the project's own MNDWI baseline on exactly the hardest lakes (Bellandur, Varthur); the unresolved licence status is a separate, non-technical risk that could block use in a formal academic submission if not clarified.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will ask directly: 'if these are the two purpose-built pretrained water models and neither was ever validated on Indian, hyacinth-choked, or seasonally-desilted lakes, why should we trust their output over your own tuned MNDWI threshold?' This is defensible only if the models are framed as a secondary, free cross-check or as one input into an ensemble alongside the baseline -- not as a stand-alone replacement -- and only once the missing-band and unclear-licence issues are disclosed and resolved rather than glossed over.
risk.honest_expectation: A fast, free, CPU-feasible secondary opinion on the water mask, useful to demonstrate that the current MNDWI baseline is not wildly inconsistent with two independently-trained external models, and cheap enough (2-4 student-days) to run purely as due diligence. It is very unlikely to be a clear net improvement on the hyacinth or desilting confounds specifically, since neither model was built to separate those cases from plain 'not water.' The realistic, defensible role for this item is as one ensemble input or one line of corroborating evidence for the baseline, not as the project's single required deep-learning deliverable.

verdict.recommended_rank: consider-with-reasons -- cheap and fast enough (2-4 student-days, CPU-only) to be worth running as a free secondary cross-check on the MNDWI baseline, but not adequate as the project's sole required deep-learning model, because neither network adds a hyacinth/vegetation class, neither has been validated on Indian or tropical urban lakes, both require a currently-missing B12 band, and both have an unresolved software licence.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: We ran the pretrained DeepWaterMap and WatNet water-detection networks as a free, zero-training cross-check against our MNDWI baseline, but did not adopt either as the project's main deep-learning model because neither separates water hyacinth from open water, neither has been validated on Indian lakes, and both need a Sentinel-2 band (B12) we had not yet cached.
